complaint: A 14-year-old girl with severe osteopetrosis, reported in her previous medical records as CLCN7-related, was referred to our tertiary center because of severe mandibular complications.

events.t: A 14-year-old girl with severe osteopetrosis, reported in her previous medical records as CLCN7-related, was referred to our tertiary center because of severe mandibular complications.
According to the medical history and documentation from the center responsible for her previous care, molecular genetic testing had identified two variants in the CLCN7 gene.

The original genetic report was not available to the authors; therefore, the exact variant nomenclature, zygosity, phase, segregation data, testing methodology, and classification could not be independently verified.
The patient was born at approximately 36 weeks of gestation by cesarean section because of fetal compromise associated with maternal hypertension, fetal growth restriction, and oligohydramnios.
Her birth weight was 1740 g, and her Apgar score was 10 points.
At seven months of age, communicating hydrocephalus, most likely posthemorrhagic, was diagnosed in the setting of increased intracranial pressure.
At eight months of age, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was implanted, and the patient remained under regular neurosurgical follow-up.

Her medical history also included long-bone fractures, optic nerve atrophy, hypothyroidism, delayed psychomotor development, previous surgical treatment of a floor-of-mouth phlegmon, and clinically evident cachexia with reduced muscle mass.
Her regular medications included levothyroxine 37.5 μg daily, vitamins B1, B6, B12, C, D, and folic acid.
The hematological manifestations of osteopetrosis were severe.

According to the available records from a previous hospitalization in a pediatric hematology department, bone marrow aspiration was unsuccessful, while trephine biopsy was technically difficult but ultimately obtained.
Histopathological examination demonstrated marked obliteration of the intertrabecular spaces by thickened bone trabeculae, with an absence of normal hematopoietic marrow.
Significant splenomegaly was also documented in the context of suspected extramedullary hematopoiesis.
Reticulocytosis of 4% was documented, while an eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) test was negative.
Elevated D-dimer concentrations were reported in the available medical records; however, the underlying cause could not be independently established from the available documentation.

According to the previous medical assessment, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation had been considered but was not pursued because of the advanced stage of disease and the patient's clinical condition.
She subsequently required hospitalization in a pediatric hematology and oncology department because of anemia and received transfusions of blood products.

According to the history obtained from the patient's mother, symptoms of mandibular inflammation and recurrent abscess formation had been present for approximately three years before admission to our institution.
During this period, the patient required repeated hospitalizations at different medical centers.
During the most recent hospitalization, the mandibular abscess was incised and drained, and necrotic tissues were debrided.
The patient was subsequently referred to our Department of Maxillofacial Surgery.
Following imaging studies, specialist consultations, and hematological preparation, removal of necrotic mandibular lesions with simultaneous submental flap reconstruction was performed.
On admission to the Department of Maxillofacial Surgery, the patient was in a relatively stable general condition but presented with marked features of advanced osteopetrosis.
Physical examination revealed significant short stature, cachexia, reduced muscle mass, and a grayish skin complexion.
There was proptosis and visual impairment.
A ventriculoperitoneal shunt was visible over the left parietal-occipital region.
Marked splenomegaly was present, with the spleen extending toward the left iliac fossa, accompanied by hepatomegaly of approximately 3-4 cm below the right costal margin.
Contractures of the lower extremity joints were also noted.
On admission, laboratory evaluation demonstrated anemia and thrombocytopenia, with a hemoglobin concentration of 8.4 g/dL and a platelet count of 61 × 10⁹/L, as shown in Table 1.

A pediatric hematology consultation recommended additional laboratory evaluation, abdominal ultrasonography, intravenous vitamin K administration, and optimization of hematological parameters before surgery.

Following hematological optimization and transfusion of blood products, the hemoglobin concentration increased to 11.7 g/dL, and the platelet count to 83 × 10⁹/L. The patient received two units of packed red blood cells and two units of platelet concentrate before surgery.
Subsequent preoperative laboratory testing is presented in Table 2.

Additional preoperative abnormalities included increased red cell distribution width (RDW), mild leukocytosis with an elevated proportion of immature granulocytes, an elevated CRP concentration of 29 mg/L (reference range <5 mg/L), and a markedly elevated D-dimer level of 5368.2 ng/mL.
The activated partial thromboplastin time was within the laboratory reference range, while fibrinogen was reported as within the normal range in the available medical records.
Computed tomography angiography of the craniofacial region demonstrated generalized marked thickening and sclerosis of the examined bones, consistent with advanced osteopetrosis.
Significant bone defects were present in the anterior mandibular body, with adjacent air bubbles interpreted as post-inflammatory and post-surgical changes, as shown in Figure 1.
Both submental arteries were patent throughout their course, and both facial arteries demonstrated contrast enhancement along their entire visualized course, as shown in Figure 2.
Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated marked splenomegaly, with the spleen measuring 189 × 95 mm and containing additional splenic tissue measuring approximately 18 mm, as shown in Figure 3.
The liver was mildly enlarged, extending approximately 28 mm below the right costal margin, with preserved parenchymal echogenicity.
A small amount of free fluid was observed in the perisplenic region and the pelvic recess.
Following induction of anesthesia, oral endotracheal intubation was performed using videolaryngoscopy, with placement of a size 6 endotracheal tube.
The patient subsequently underwent surgical treatment of the mandibular lesion, including intraoral osteotomy and removal of necrotic mandibular bone with debridement of the affected tissues.
Simultaneous reconstruction of the anterior floor of the mouth was performed using a submental flap.
The flap was harvested through a submental incision and included the platysma and anterior belly of the digastric muscle.
The facial vessels were identified and preserved, and the submandibular gland was mobilized.
Following intraoral debridement and preparation of the mucosal margins, a tunnel was created through the floor of the mouth, and the flap was transferred intraorally.
The skin paddle was positioned within the tissue defect and securely sutured.

The procedure did not involve segmental mandibular resection; the necrotic mandibular bone was removed by intraoral osteotomy and debridement, without intentional interruption of mandibular continuity.
No bony reconstruction or fixation was required
Histopathological examination of the submandibular lymph node demonstrated reactive changes, with preserved follicular architecture, reactive lymphoid follicles, and sinus histiocytosis.
Histopathological examination of the submandibular gland demonstrated periductal and interlobular fibrosis with scattered individual lymphocytes.

The clinical course of the patient, from the systemic manifestations of CLCN7-related osteopetrosis to mandibular involvement, surgical treatment, and postoperative management, is summarized in Figure 4.

Postoperatively, the patient developed significant soft-tissue edema with concern for upper airway obstruction and was therefore transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) while intubated and mechanically ventilated.
Oral endotracheal intubation had been performed using videolaryngoscopy, with placement of a size 6 endotracheal tube.
On admission to the PICU, she remained under analgosedation.
Physical examination demonstrated marked cachexia and reduced muscle mass, grayish skin coloration, proptosis, and pronounced hepatosplenomegaly.
A postoperative neck dressing and Redon drain were present, with only a small amount of blood in the drain.
The preoperative intraoral appearance and the early postoperative result following removal of the necrotic mandibular bone and reconstruction with a submental flap are shown in Figure 5.
Analgesia and sedation were maintained with midazolam and sufentanil, with ketamine also used perioperatively.

Mechanical ventilation was continued using synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation with pressure control (SIMV-PC mode) with an initial FiO₂ of 0.30, with ventilatory parameters adjusted according to serial blood-gas analyses.
Cardiovascular status remained stable, with a tendency toward mild hypertension managed pharmacologically.
Fluid therapy was adjusted according to the patient's clinical status, with diuresis supported by fractionated doses of furosemide.
Enteral nutritional support with Nutrini was provided during the perioperative period.
In accordance with the pediatric hematology recommendations, deferoxamine was administered to reduce the risk of excessive iron accumulation associated with repeated blood transfusions.
Antibiotic therapy was initially administered empirically and was subsequently adjusted according to antimicrobial susceptibility results.
During the perioperative period, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and metronidazole were continued.
On the third postoperative day, sedation was discontinued, and the patient was successfully extubated.
She subsequently maintained spontaneous breathing with passive oxygen therapy.
Her respiratory and cardiovascular status remained stable, and the postoperative edema gradually decreased.
The surgical wounds demonstrated satisfactory early healing without documented acute postoperative complications.
After stabilization, the patient was transferred from the PICU to the Department of Head and Neck Surgery for Children and Adolescents for continued postoperative care.
The available documentation covers the early postoperative period; long-term clinical and radiological follow-up was not available.

pearls: In the present patient, transplantation had previously been considered but was ultimately not pursued.
Therefore, the surgical approach should be individualized according to the extent of necrotic bone, severity of infection, systemic condition, and potential for adequate soft-tissue healing.
In the present case, avoiding segmental mandibular resection was an important treatment consideration.

Given the patient's anemia, thrombocytopenia, clinically evident cachexia, and limited physiological reserve, extensive mandibular resection was considered potentially associated with substantial morbidity.
Postoperative airway edema should be considered multifactorial.

src.title: Submental Flap Reconstruction for Mandibular Osteomyelitis in an Adolescent Patient With Osteopetrosis: A Case Report
src.authors: Jeremi Matysek, Dominika Lech, Robert Maksymowicz et al.

complaint: We report the case of a 33-year-old right-handed unemployed male, living in precarious socioeconomic conditions with active chronic alcohol and tobacco use.

events.t: We report the case of a 33-year-old right-handed unemployed male, living in precarious socioeconomic conditions with active chronic alcohol and tobacco use.
The patient had no significant surgical history and was not receiving any addiction treatment prior to the trauma.
In July 2024, the patient was admitted to the emergency department three hours after sustaining complex multi-tissue right elbow trauma from a broken glass laceration in a suicide attempt.
Initial examination revealed an intoxicated patient presenting with severe hemorrhagic shock, with blood pressure of 60/30 mmHg and tachycardia of 140 beats per minute.
Vascular examination revealed a deep wound on the medial aspect of the distal third of the right arm with active bleeding and hematoma.

The right upper extremity showed acute ischemia characterized by cyanosis and distal coldness, absent radial and ulnar pulses confirmed by absent Doppler flow, and digital saturation collapsed at 80%.
Standard elbow radiographs revealed no bone abnormalities.
The complete injury assessment, established after hemodynamic stabilization and surgical exploration, revealed an exceptional combination of major injuries detailed in Table 1.
Complete brachial artery transection was responsible for active hemorrhage and distal ischemia.
Associated injuries included complete median nerve neurotmesis at the elbow level, complete distal biceps tendon rupture, and extensive cutaneous wound exposing vital/neurovascular structures.
Preoperative brain computed tomography scan, motivated by associated head trauma, revealed frontal contusion requiring prophylactic antiepileptic treatment with carbamazepine for one month.
Emergency surgical management was performed within a remarkably short four-hour window, requiring close collaboration between vascular and orthopedic surgery teams.
Vascular reconstruction consisted of brachial-to-brachial bypass using an 8-cm reversed saphenous vein autograft.
After hemorrhage control with an Esmarch bandage and systemic heparinization, proximal and distal end-to-end anastomoses were performed using 6/0 Prolene suture.
Graft patency was verified by Fogarty catheter passage, retrieving no thrombus, with immediate recovery of distal pulses.
Nerve repair was performed by direct end-to-end median nerve suture; the absence of substance loss eliminated the need for nerve grafting.
Epiperineurial suture was performed with 6/0 Prolene monofilament.
Distal biceps tendon repair was achieved by end-to-end suture with cardinal solidarization stitches.
The procedure concluded with careful debridement and layered skin closure.
The immediate postoperative course was uncomplicated with maintained satisfactory distal vascularization.
Initial assessment at one month postoperatively shows limitation of elbow flexion to 130° and extension to -60° in pronation and supination.

Clinical examination revealed complete paralysis of thumb and index distal interphalangeal flexion, rated 0/5 on the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale, as well as total thumb opposition paralysis indicating complete thenar eminence involvement.
These deficits rendered functional thumb-index pinch impossible.
Sensory examination showed permanent paresthesias affecting the entire median nerve territory, involving the first three finger pulps and radial half of the fourth finger.

Initial functional assessment using validated outcome measures revealed severe disability with a Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) score of 78, indicating significant functional impairment in activities of daily living (ADL).

During this initial period, we encountered poor therapeutic compliance; the patient showed minimal engagement in the rehabilitation program and categorically refused psychiatric or addiction follow-up despite repeated recommendations.
The three-month postoperative assessment revealed major neurological sequelae summarized in Table 2.

Analytical examination revealed complete paralysis of the thumb and index distal interphalangeal flexion, rated 0/5 on the MRC scale, as well as total thumb opposition paralysis, indicating complete thenar eminence involvement.
These deficits rendered functional thumb-index pinch impossible.
Sensory examination showed permanent paresthesias affecting the entire median nerve territory, involving the first three finger pulps and radial half of the fourth finger.
Joint examination revealed significant elbow stiffness with preserved flexion at 150° but extension limited to -30°, associated with slight pronation limitation.
Inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joints of the thumb and index finger was noted, with a tendency toward metacarpophalangeal hyperextension during active finger extension.
Neurological examination found a positive Tinel sign at the suture site at the elbow, an encouraging sign indicating early axonal regeneration.
Distal vascularization remained satisfactory with well-perceived radial and ulnar pulses.
Electroneuromyography (ENMG) performed in October 2024, three months post trauma, confirmed nerve injury severity.

Nerve conduction studies showed a complete absence of motor and sensory response of the right median nerve, contrasting with strictly normal electrophysiological parameters for the ipsilateral ulnar nerve.

Needle ENMG revealed intense pathological spontaneous activity in flexor carpi radialis and abductor pollicis brevis, with a poor microvolt neurogenic pattern for the latter and a rich neurogenic pattern with high amplitude potentials for flexor carpi radialis.
These findings confirmed complete right median nerve neurotmesis at elbow level with active denervation of tributary muscles.
Clinical evaluation at three months showed modest improvement in elbow range of motion with a persistent -30° extension deficit.
Fine motor deficits remained unchanged.
However, the Tinel sign had progressed to the upper third of the forearm, indicating nerve regeneration progression at approximately 1 mm per day.
The functional score showed modest improvement with DASH decreasing to 65.
A significant turning point in evolution was observed at the December 2024 assessment.
Clinical examination revealed partial thumb opposition recovery, allowing functional thumb-index pinch initiation.
The Tinel sign had continued progression, reaching the middle third of the forearm.

Electrophysiological evolution was particularly encouraging with reappearance of motor potentials still of low amplitude (0.31 mV at wrist and 0.15 mV at arm) but with measurable conduction velocity at 45.1 m/s.
Sensory conduction also showed recovery signs with reappearance of sensory potentials of 0.41 µV amplitude and conduction velocity of 34.0 m/s.
This neurophysiological improvement was accompanied by significant functional progress, with DASH score improving to 45.
Complete evolution of electrophysiological parameters throughout follow-up is summarized in Table 3, showing remarkable nerve recovery progression.
Concurrently, detailed clinical-functional evolution in Table 4 illustrates a correlation between electrophysiological data and functional recovery.

The patient's clinical course from initial trauma to complete recovery is illustrated in Figure 5, providing a comprehensive visual timeline of functional outcomes and key milestones over the 12-month follow-up period.

This timeline demonstrates the progressive improvement in DASH scores from 78/100 at one month to 18/100 at 12 months, correlating with the structured three-phase rehabilitation protocol described in Table 5.
It is important to emphasize that the patient's therapeutic compliance markedly improved after the third month, coinciding with the appearance of the first objective signs of neurological recovery.
This improvement in rehabilitation program adherence likely played a determining role in subsequent favorable evolution.
Final assessment performed in July 2025, one year after initial trauma, revealed remarkable functional recovery.
Clinical examination found only mild residual paresthesias in the median nerve territory, with the patient having recovered complete motor function.

Finger flexion demonstrated good recovery of thumb and index distal interphalangeal flexion, with total recovery of thumb opposition allowing functional thumb-index pinch, symmetrical to the contralateral side.
Elbow range of motion was normalized with complete extension at 0° and preserved flexion at 150°.
Grip function was symmetrical to the contralateral side, allowing complete autonomy for all ADL.
Final clinical photographs demonstrate this exceptional recovery.
Final electrophysiological evolution was exceptional with near-complete normalization of all median nerve parameters.
Motor amplitude at the wrist reached 3.2 mV, approaching normal limits, with near-normalized conduction velocities both distally (69.6 m/s) and proximally at Erb's point (71.3 m/s).
Amplitude was also preserved throughout the nerve course, measured at 3.5 mV at the elbow crease and 3.4 mV at the arm, demonstrating homogeneous recovery without residual conduction block.
Sensory conduction was nearly normalized with amplitude at 1.1 µV and conduction velocity at 54.8 m/s.

This remarkable neurophysiological recovery translated into excellent final functional outcomes with a DASH score of 18, indicating near-normal upper extremity function and supporting potential return to work.
Rehabilitation management was structured around a protocol organized in three distinct phases, progressively adapted to patient clinical evolution and therapeutic compliance improvement.

The early phase primarily targeted post-traumatic edema control, joint range of motion maintenance, and perineural adhesion prevention, crucial elements for creating favorable tissue conditions for nerve regeneration.

The intermediate phase, beginning with appearance of first reinnervation signs, progressively introduced adapted muscle strengthening and specific sensory reeducation according to neuronal plasticity principles.
The late phase focused on functional optimization with intensive work on strengthening, coordination, and readaptation to specific professional gestures.
A personalized daily self-program systematically complemented supervised sessions at each phase, maximizing neuromotor stimulation and patient active involvement in recovery.
Detailed modalities of this protocol are presented in Table 5.

pearls: This global approach corresponds to current recommendations for complex upper extremity trauma management.

Spectacular improvement in rehabilitation program adherence after the third month, precisely coinciding with the appearance of the first objective neurological recovery signs, emphasizes the crucial importance of psychological factors in the recovery process.
The socioeconomic impact of this recovery is considerable when considering that forearm nerve injuries result in job loss in nearly a quarter of cases, according to literature data.
Despite these exceptional results, several limitations must be emphasized.
Absence of structured psychiatric follow-up, despite our repeated recommendations, represents a missed opportunity for global management optimization.

src.title: Exceptional Complete Functional Recovery After Severe Multitissue Elbow Trauma in a Suicide Attempt Context: A Case Report
src.authors: Mohamed Harmouche, Mohammed Maroc, Abdelilah Rhoul et al.

complaint: A healthy 26-year-old pregnant woman (39 weeks and 3 days) underwent an elective cesarean delivery due to breech presentation.

events.t: A healthy 26-year-old pregnant woman (39 weeks and 3 days) underwent an elective cesarean delivery due to breech presentation.
A subarachnoid block (8 mg of bupivacaine 0.5% and 2.5 mcg of sufentanil; height 162 cm) was administered, and after 5 min, hypotension, nausea, and headache ensued.
Ten milligrams of ephedrine were given without response.
Subsequently, 2 mg of phenylephrine was incorrectly administered due to a dilution error that went undetected at the time.
Hypotension continued to worsen and bradycardia developed, leading to 0.5 mg of atropine being administered.
Soon after, the patient developed a dry cough and reported a headache.
At this point, hypertension and sinus tachycardia were present and oxygen saturation dropped (minimum SatO2 92%).
Crackles were present on auscultation, and hypoxemia was noted on analysis of blood gases (partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2), pH, and other parameters were normal).
No other signs or symptoms were found on clinical assessment.
Supportive treatment was immediately initiated.
It included oxygen by a non-rebreather face mask and intravenous furosemide at a dose of 40 mg, which allowed completion of the surgery.
Meanwhile, the anesthesia team members (ATMs), an anesthesia nurse, and an anesthesiologist reviewed recent events and detected the dilution error.
At our institution, drugs are generally prepared by the anesthesia nurse, and since phenylephrine is only available as a 10 mg/mL ampoule, this drug must be diluted twice.
The first dilution yields a 1 mg/mL solution, and a second dilution yields a 0.1 mg/mL solution, which is normally used for boluses.
For cesarian deliveries under spinal anesthesia, this preparation is done beforehand.
However, in this case, only the first dilution was completed.
In other words, the syringe containing 1 mg/mL of phenylephrine was used, thus, the delivered dose was 10 times higher than intended.
As the ATMs were trying to correct the hypotension as quickly as possible, the drug was given without further checking.
This inadvertently higher dose of phenylephrine was thought to explain the constellation of signs and symptoms that were observed.
Nonetheless, it was mandatory to exclude potentially life-threatening conditions, including APEd, myocardial infarction, and pulmonary embolism.
The 12-lead EKG had no abnormalities.
The blood analysis revealed normocytic, normochromic anemia and mildly elevated cardiac necrosis markers while N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-Pro-BNP) was negative.
Point-of-care cardiac ultrasound revealed hypokinesia of the inferior septal wall of the left ventricle, with no other changes.
A computed tomography (CT) angiography revealed no sign of embolism.
However, the CT demonstrated bilateral parenchymal infiltration in a ground-glass pattern, compatible with hemorrhage, as well as a thin layer of pulmonary effusion bilaterally.
Owing to these findings, the intensive care, obstetrics, and radiology teams were involved.
The decision was made to have the patient remain in the postanesthetic care unit to receive monitoring and supportive treatment.
A debriefing was performed by the ATM, under nonjudgmental terms, to address the dilution error and to delineate strategies to avoid its recurrence.

Such strategies included label checks by a second person, implementing the “five rights” of administration (the right patient, the right drug, the right dose, the right route, and the right time), closed-loop communication while administering drugs, and discarding of drugs with indefinite content.
The patient’s condition evolved favorably within 24 h, in terms of clinical assessment and laboratory parameters.
A CT scan was repeated on Day 4 and revealed the resolution of the described infiltrates.

Blood markers for pulmonary capillaritis were all negative, including testing for antinuclear antibodies (extractable nuclear antigen screen, anti-double-stranded DNA, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies) and perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (anti-myeloperoxidase and anti-proteinase 3).
Discharge occurred six days after the event.
An internal medicine appointment was set for a month later to follow up on the patient, but she missed it.
To our knowledge, she did not require any other medical care, and the well-being of the neonate was not affected by this event.

pearls: Since these errors are preventable and could have fatal consequences, patient safety should be a priority in the operating room.
The case demonstrates how a quick review of events is crucial for errors to be identified, which can prevent future accidents, as well as foster team building and trust among workers.

We would like to stress that notification of this adverse drug event to the pharmaceutical company should have been carried out afterward to bring attention to a formula with a high potential for error.
